title: Path Sum: given a tree and a target, determine if any root-to-leaf path sums to the target. Path Sum III: count the number of downward paths (not necessarily starting at the root or ending at a leaf) whose values sum to the target.
shortTitle: Path Sum / Path Sum III — root-to-leaf path / all downward paths summing to target

s1_definition.profdef: Path Sum asks whether a root-to-leaf path exists whose node values add up to a target, solved by a depth-first recursion that subtracts each node's value and checks for the remainder at a leaf. Path Sum III generalizes to counting all downward paths summing to the target, solved efficiently with a prefix-sum HashMap that, at each node, counts how many earlier prefixes along the current root path equal the running sum minus the target.
s1_definition.analogy: Path Sum is like asking whether any single chain of command from the branch manager down to a frontline employee has salaries adding up to exactly a budget figure. Path Sum III is harder: it counts every downward stretch of the chain, not just full ones from top to bottom, whose salaries hit the figure. To count those efficiently, as you walk down a chain you remember every running total you have seen so far, so when the current total overshoots the target by an amount you have seen before, you know a matching stretch ends right here.
s1_definition.oneliner: Path Sum subtracts toward a leaf; Path Sum III uses a running prefix sum and a HashMap so each node counts matching downward paths in constant time.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Path Sum asks whether a root-to-leaf path exists whose node values add up to a target, solved by a depth-first recursion that subtracts each node's value and checks for the remainder at a leaf. Path Sum III generalizes to counting all downward paths summing to the target, solved efficiently with a prefix-sum HashMap that, at each node, counts how many earlier prefixes along the current root path equal the running sum minus the target.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Path Sum is like asking whether any single chain of command from the branch manager down to a frontline employee has salaries adding up to exactly a budget figure. Path Sum III is harder: it counts every downward stretch of the chain, not just full ones from top to bottom, whose salaries hit the figure. To count those efficiently, as you walk down a chain you remember every running total you have seen so far, so when the current total overshoots the target by an amount you have seen before, you know a matching stretch ends right here.

**One line to remember:** Path Sum subtracts toward a leaf; Path Sum III uses a running prefix sum and a HashMap so each node counts matching downward paths in constant time.

sections.s2_technical:
Path Sum is the simpler of the two. You recurse down, subtracting the current node's value from the remaining target, and at a leaf you check whether the remainder is exactly the node's value, meaning the path hit the target. For example: `if (node.left == null && node.right == null) return remaining == node.val;`, after which you recurse into children with `remaining - node.val`. It returns true if either branch succeeds, so it is a linear traversal that short-circuits on the first matching path.

Path Sum III is where the technique matters. A naive solution would, from every node, explore all downward paths, which is order n times height. The efficient approach uses prefix sums. As you walk a root-to-current path, you maintain the running sum from the root to the current node. A downward path ending at the current node and summing to the target exists exactly when some ancestor had a prefix sum equal to the current running sum minus the target, because the difference between the two prefixes is the path between them.

You keep a HashMap from prefix-sum value to how many times it has occurred on the current root path. At each node you compute the running sum, then add the count of `runningSum - target` from the map to the answer. For example: `count += prefixCounts.getOrDefault(runningSum - target, 0);`. You then record the current running sum in the map, recurse into both children, and crucially remove the current running sum from the map when backtracking, so counts do not leak across sibling branches. For example: `prefixCounts.merge(runningSum, 1, Integer::sum); ...recurse...; prefixCounts.merge(runningSum, -1, Integer::sum);`.

You seed the map with prefix sum zero having count one, which handles paths that start at the root. The time complexity is linear because each node is visited once with constant-time map operations, down from the naive quadratic. A senior nuance is the backtracking step: forgetting to decrement the map on the way back up double-counts paths from unrelated branches, and using long for the running sum avoids overflow with large values.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a tree represents a chain of linked transactions, each carrying an amount, and fraud detection wants to know whether any full chain from the origin down to a terminal account sums to a flagged amount. This is exactly how Path Sum works — a root-to-leaf sum check.

Problem 2 — More powerfully, fraud detection wants to count every downward sub-chain, not just full ones, that sums to the flagged amount, because structured laundering hides the target inside a longer chain. This is exactly how Path Sum III works, and the prefix-sum HashMap makes counting all such sub-chains linear.

The mini-project builds a `TxnNode` class with an integer amount, a `PathSumService` with both the root-to-leaf check and the prefix-sum counting method with logging, and a runnable demo over a transaction chain tree.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is the transaction chain tree and a target of eight. The famous example counts three downward sub-chains summing to eight.

Step 1: For Path Sum, the recursion subtracts from the target along each root-to-leaf chain. Starting at ten, remaining is minus two, then down the left to five, three, three, and so on; the check succeeds only if some full chain from the root to a leaf lands exactly at zero remaining. In this tree a full origin-to-terminal chain summing to eight does not exist, so Path Sum returns false.

Step 2: For Path Sum III, the prefix map starts with prefix sum zero counted once. At the root ten, the running sum is ten, and it looks for ten minus eight equals two in the map, which is absent, so no path ends here. It records ten in the map.

Step 3: Descending to five, the running sum is fifteen, and it looks for fifteen minus eight equals seven, absent. It records fifteen. Descending to three, running sum eighteen, looks for ten, absent, records eighteen. Descending to the leaf three, running sum twenty-one, looks for thirteen, absent. Descending to minus two instead, running sum sixteen, looks for eight, absent. These particular stretches do not match, but the three matching stretches in the classic example are five then three, the five-three-three chain's internal segment, and the minus-three then eleven chain, each of which sums to eight and is counted the moment its ending node computes a running sum whose difference from an earlier recorded prefix equals eight.

Step 4: The crucial backtracking: when the recursion returns from a node, it decrements that node's running sum from the map, so when it explores a sibling branch the prefixes from the abandoned branch no longer count. This prevents paths that cross between unrelated branches from being falsely counted.

Step 5: After visiting every node with the prefix-sum technique, the total number of downward sub-chains summing to eight is three.

```text
2026-10-26T20:10:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Transaction Chain Path Sums
2026-10-26T20:10:00Z [INFO] Full origin-to-terminal chain summing to 8? false
2026-10-26T20:10:00Z [INFO] Total downward sub-chains summing to 8 = 3
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
              10
            /    \
           5      -3
          / \       \
         3   2       11
        / \   \
       3  -2   1       target = 8

  Path Sum (root→leaf): subtract along each chain, check leaf==0
    no full chain hits 8 → false

  Path Sum III (prefix-sum map):
    prefix{0:1} seeded
    at each node: runningSum += amount
                  paths += prefix[runningSum - 8]
                  prefix[runningSum]++
                  recurse L,R
                  prefix[runningSum]--   ← BACKTRACK (no cross-branch leak)
    matching downward sub-chains: 3 total 
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Path Sum and Path Sum III are a pair that shows how a small change in the question demands a very different technique. Path Sum asks only whether a full root-to-leaf chain adds up to a target, and that is a straightforward depth-first recursion where I subtract each node's value from the remaining target and, at a leaf, check whether the remainder is exactly zero. It returns true on the first matching chain, so it is linear and short-circuits.

Path Sum III is harder, because it counts every downward path, not just full ones, that sums to the target. The naive approach explores all paths from every node and is quadratic. My efficient solution uses prefix sums: as I walk the current root-to-node path I keep a running sum, and a downward path ending at the current node hits the target exactly when some ancestor had a prefix sum equal to the running sum minus the target, because the gap between those two prefixes is the path between them. I keep a HashMap from prefix-sum value to its occurrence count on the current path, add the count of running-sum-minus-target at each node, and seed the map with zero counted once so root-starting paths are included.

The step that separates people who understand it from people who memorized it is the backtracking: when I return from a node I decrement its running sum from the map, so the prefixes of an abandoned branch never leak into a sibling branch and inflate the count. I also use a long running sum to avoid overflow. This brings the whole count down to linear time.

In my project at National Bank of India, I modeled a chain of linked transactions as a tree where each node carries an amount, and fraud detection used both methods. Path Sum answered whether a full origin-to-terminal chain matched a flagged amount, while Path Sum III counted every downward sub-chain summing to that amount, because structured laundering hides the target inside a longer chain. The prefix-sum map with correct backtracking made scanning large transaction chains fast and accurate, flagging exactly the sub-chains that summed to the suspicious figure.
